I always use https://pcpartpicker.com for system builds. It's just easy. The prices for Z390 boards are pretty close to what you've listed there... but if you sort by price, you can find cheaper ones like this.

And if price is a factor, you could get a 1700 series and save over $100 - and you can always upgrade to a 2700x on the same motherboard sometime in the future because they're both on the AM4 socket.

Ryzen is much closer to Intel in gaming performance than people here are giving it credit for: https://www.techspot.com/review/1655-core-i7-8700k-vs-ryzen-7-2700x/

They are both overclocked, but mind you the 8700k has an 800mhz advantage. Granted the 2700x at 4.2ghz is below the maximum 4.3ghz boost frequency. You also get 8 cores instead of 6, and there's a big sale going on for Ryzen right now. You can get 2700 for $260 on newegg right now, and 2700x for $299.

AMD has committed to bringing the next gen Ryzen to the same socket, and there's rumors that the entire line is going to get more cores (3700x would be 12 or 16 core for the same price).

If you are going to keep your computer for a long time, you'll get more out of it from a Ryzen system. If it's strictly for gaming you might be better off with the 8700k, but if you're doing other things, those extra cores and the lower price is worth it. Don't forget the higher resolution you're gaming at, the less the CPU matters. If you're at 1080p you might feel a difference, but at 4k it's basically entirely GPU limited and the CPU won't matter as much. If it's something silly, like a core i3 with a 1080 Ti you'll have problems. But something like choosing between a $350 Ryzen and a $350 Intel isn't going to make a huge difference. You can even get a first gen Ryzen 1700 for $170 right now on Newegg.

There will always be games optimized for AMD and some for Intel. Even in AMD's last glory days, they had games where Pentium 4 would crush Athlon. It's just how it works when you're comparing two different microarchs. So you'll see AMD pull ahead some times, and other times not do so well. But it's always been like that. Even AMD's crappy FX 8000 series had games when it did exceptionally well (for the price at least).

AMD has some good CPUs right now and they're worth it. I've been using a Ryzen 1700x for the last two years and it's been great to me. Planning on dropping the new Ryzen in the same motherboard when it comes out, something you can never do with an Intel.
